doc.title: John Beal interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 18, 2024

chapter: Studio work and learning the craft
title: How New York studio work came in
summary: Work came by word of mouth and contractors; Beal worked for nearly everyone and usually knew little about a date beforehand.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: How does that work — in the heyday of the studio scene in New York, do you get hooked up with a contractor, establish a reputation and then your phone starts to ring?

It’s mostly word of mouth you know, but you do get hooked up with contractors who can depend on what you do because a lot of times they’ll book something and the requirements aren’t fully known and if you’re versatile, and they know you can cover a variety of styles and situations, you know, they want to hire you, you know, so they’re covered. And I was lucky enough to be called by several different contractors and I worked for almost everybody. I didn’t have any particular affiliation you know.
Did you typically know what you were in for when you showed up at a studio for a date? Did they tell you this is a cigarette commercial or this is a pop recording date for a singer?

No. You’d get called, they give you the time and what instrument. That’s it. You know but a record date you’d find out what it is, you’d get a good idea of what to expect. You know like if you’re doing an album, if it’s a show album or a singer or, you know, whatever.
